module_title: Mechanics II - Moment of Inertia & Gravitational Field (Intermediate)
introduction: This level focuses on the mathematical calculations of Rotational Inertia, Torque, and how the acceleration due to gravity ($g$) varies with depth, height, and the Earth's rotation.

core_concepts.title: Moment of Inertia ($I$)
core_concepts.description: The rotational equivalent of mass (inertia). It depends not just on the mass, but on how that mass is distributed relative to the axis of rotation ($I = \sum m r^2$).

core_concepts.title: Axis Theorems
core_concepts.description: Parallel Axis Theorem: $I = I_{\text{com}} + Md^2$ (valid for all 2D/3D shapes). Perpendicular Axis Theorem: $I_z = I_x + I_y$ (strictly valid ONLY for 2D planar laminas).

core_concepts.title: Torque ($\tau$)
core_concepts.description: The turning effect of a force. Calculated as $\tau = \vec{r} \times \vec{F}$ or $\tau = I\alpha$. For a body to be in total equilibrium, both net force and net torque must be zero.

core_concepts.title: Variation of 'g'
core_concepts.description: At height $h$ above surface: $g' = g(1 - 2h/R)$ (only if $h \ll R$). At depth $d$ below surface: $g' = g(1 - d/R)$. At the exact center of the Earth, $g = 0$.

important_entities.name: Angular Momentum ($L$)
important_entities.significance: The rotational equivalent of linear momentum. It is strictly conserved when the net external torque on the system is zero.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Do NOT apply $I_z = I_x + I_y$ to 3D objects like spheres, cylinders, or cones. It only works for flat, 2D objects like rings, discs, and rectangular plates.

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: Ring is Full ($MR^2$), Disc is Half ($MR^2/2$)
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: For an axis passing through the center and perpendicular to the plane, a Ring has a moment of inertia of $MR^2$, while a solid Disc is $MR^2/2$.

exam_strategy_tips: In height variation problems, if $h$ is greater than 5% of Earth's radius ($R$), do not use the approximation $(1-2h/R)$. Use the exact formula: $g' = g / (1 + h/R)^2$.
